summary.text: For any positive period \(T\), evaluating at \(0\) and \(1\) and expanding \((T+1)^p\) shows \(n\mid T^p\) and \(n\mid pTU\), where primality makes all intermediate binomial coefficients divisible by \(p\) and \(U\) is coprime to \(n\); hence \(n\mid pT\), which forces \(n/p\mid T\) if \(p^2\mid n\) and \(n\mid T\) otherwise. Conversely, \(n\) is always a period, while when \(p^2\mid n\), the binomial expansion shows that \(n/p\) is a period because every nonconstant term is divisible by \(n\), giving the claimed minima.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(n\ge 1\). Define
\[
\mathcal P_{p,n}=\{T\in\mathbb N:T>0\text{ and }(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n\text{ for every }k\in\mathbb N\}.
\]
Thus the period length \(a_p(n)\) is the least element of \(\mathcal P_{p,n}\). This set is nonempty: \(n\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\), because \(k+n\equiv k\pmod n\), and therefore
\((k+n)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n\) for every \(k\). Since every nonempty set of natural numbers has a least element, the period length is well-defined.

We will prove
\[
a_p(n)=
\begin{cases}
n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\]
The main step is a necessary divisibility condition on every possible period.

### Lemma: every period \(T\) satisfies \(n\mid pT\)

Fix \(T\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\). Substituting \(k=0\) into the period congruence gives
\[
T^p\equiv 0^p=0\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
n\mid T^p. \tag{1}
\]

Next substitute \(k=1\). We obtain
\[
(1+T)^p\equiv 1\pmod n. \tag{2}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, for every integer \(j\) with \(1\le j\le p-1\), the binomial coefficient \(\binom pj\) is divisible by \(p\). In particular, for \(2\le j\le p-1\), write
\[
\binom pj=p c_j
\]
with \(c_j\in\mathbb N\). (When \(p=2\), the range \(2\le j\le p-1\) is empty.) The binomial theorem then gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1+T)^p
 &=1+pT+\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}\binom pjT^j+T^p\\
 &=1+T^p+pT\left(1+\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}c_jT^{j-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Set
\[
U=1+\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}c_jT^{j-1}.
\]
Using (1) in congruence (2), the terms \(1\) and \(T^p\) may be removed, yielding
\[
pTU\equiv0\pmod n,
\]
or equivalently
\[
n\mid pTU. \tag{3}
\]

We claim that \(\gcd(n,U)=1\). Suppose otherwise. Then some prime \(q\) divides both \(n\) and \(U\). From \(q\mid n\) and (1), we have \(q\mid T^p\). Since \(q\) is prime, this implies \(q\mid T\). Every term
\(c_jT^{j-1}\) in the sum defining \(U\) is consequently divisible by \(q\), because \(j-1\ge1\). Hence
\[
U=1+\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}c_jT^{j-1}\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
But \(q\mid U\) would also give \(U\equiv0\pmod q\), a contradiction. Thus \(n\) and \(U\) are coprime.

Now (3), together with \(\gcd(n,U)=1\), implies by Euclid's lemma that
\[
n\mid pT. \tag{4}
\]
This proves the lemma.

We now treat the two cases in the statement.

### Case 1: \(p^2\mid n\)

Write
\[
n=p^2m
\]
for some positive integer \(m\). Then
\[
\frac np=pm.
\]
Set
\[
T_0=\frac np=pm.
\]
We first show that \(T_0\) is a period. Notice that
\[
pT_0=n \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
T_0^2=p^2m^2=nm, \tag{6}
\]
so \(n\mid T_0^2\).

For any \(k\in\mathbb N\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
(k+T_0)^p-k^p
 =pT_0k^{p-1}+\sum_{j=2}^{p}\binom pjT_0^jk^{p-j}. \tag{7}
\]
The first term on the right is divisible by \(n\), by (5). Every term in the sum is also divisible by \(n\), because it contains \(T_0^j\) with \(j\ge2\), and (6) says that \(n\mid T_0^2\). Therefore the entire right-hand side of (7) is divisible by \(n\). Thus
\[
(k+T_0)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\). Since \(T_0>0\), this proves \(T_0\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\), and hence
\[
a_p(n)\le \frac np. \tag{8}
\]

Conversely, let \(T\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\) be any positive period. By the lemma, \(n\mid pT\). Since \(p\mid n\), write \(n=p(n/p)\). We then have
\[
p\left(\frac np\right)\mid pT.
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(p\) gives
\[
\frac np\mid T.
\]
Because \(T>0\), it follows that \(T\ge n/p\). In particular, the least positive period satisfies
\[
a_p(n)\ge\frac np. \tag{9}
\]
Combining (8) and (9) gives
\[
a_p(n)=\frac np
\]
when \(p^2\mid n\).

### Case 2: \(p^2\nmid n\)

As observed at the beginning, \(n\) itself is always a period, so
\[
a_p(n)\le n. \tag{10}
\]
It remains to show that every positive period is at least \(n\). Let \(T\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\). We already know
\[
n\mid pT \tag{11}
\]
and, from evaluation at \(k=0\),
\[
n\mid T^p. \tag{12}
\]
We split according to whether \(p\) divides \(n\).

#### Subcase 2a: \(p\nmid n\)

Since \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(n\), we have \(\gcd(n,p)=1\). From \(n\mid pT\), Euclid's lemma therefore gives
\[
n\mid T.
\]
As \(T>0\), this implies \(T\ge n\).

#### Subcase 2b: \(p\mid n\)

Write
\[
n=pd.
\]
The assumption \(p^2\nmid n\) implies \(p\nmid d\): indeed, if \(p\mid d\), then \(d=pe\) for some \(e\), and \(n=pd=p^2e\), contrary to the hypothesis. Since \(p\) is prime, it follows that
\[
\gcd(p,d)=1. \tag{13}
\]

From (11),
\[
pd=n\mid pT.
\]
Cancelling \(p>0\) gives
\[
d\mid T. \tag{14}
\]
On the other hand, (12) and \(p\mid n\) imply \(p\mid T^p\). A prime dividing a power divides its base, so
\[
p\mid T. \tag{15}
\]
Since \(p\) and \(d\) are coprime by (13), the simultaneous divisibilities (14) and (15) imply
\[
pd\mid T.
\]
But \(pd=n\), so again \(n\mid T\), and hence \(T\ge n\).

Thus in both subcases every positive period is at least \(n\). Together with (10), this yields
\[
a_p(n)=n
\]
whenever \(p^2\nmid n\).

Combining the two main cases proves that for every prime \(p\) and every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle a_p(n)=
\begin{cases}
n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}}
\]
In particular, for cubes one takes \(p=3\): the period of \(k^3\bmod n\) is \(n/3\) when \(9\mid n\), and is \(n\) otherwise, which is the formula for OEIS A282779.
